## Downloading fastq files

As required in the assignment, first we downloaded the FASTQ files from NCBI using the fastq-dump command with the flags:
1. gzip: Compresses output using gzip.
2. split-files: Splits FASTQ reads into two files according to the 2 adapters.
3. X: Download the first X spots of a FASTQ file, in our case the first 3000000 spots.
4. O: Download output to a given path.
Below is a sample of the first 5 commands out of the 27 commands performed on each file in the file list in the SraRunTable.HW5.Fixed.txt file. 

```{r, engine='bash', Downloading fastq files from NCBI, engine='bash'}
fastq-dump --gzip --split-files -X 3000000 -O /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/data ERR031027
fastq-dump --gzip --split-files -X 3000000 -O /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/data ERR031028
fastq-dump --gzip --split-files -X 3000000 -O /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/data ERR031029
fastq-dump --gzip --split-files -X 3000000 -O /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/data ERR031030
fastq-dump --gzip --split-files -X 3000000 -O /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/data ERR031031
```

The fastqc analysis of sample 14's normal tissue indicated that the quality of sequencing is not good in this tissue. Hence, in order to maintain the comparison of normal to cancerous tissues, both tissues of sample 14 were removed.

We will use the following bash code to perform fastp: 

```{r, engine='bash', Performing fastp on all the files excluding sample 14 using the following bash code}
#!/bin/bash

# Directory containing your FASTQ files
FASTQ_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/data"

# Output directory for processed FASTQ files
OUTPUT_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/after_fastp"

# Create output directory if it doesn't exist
mkdir -p "${OUTPUT_DIR}"

# Exclude sample 14's FASTQ files
EXCLUDE_FILES=("ERR031025_1.fastq.gz" "ERR031025_2.fastq.gz" "ERR031026_1.fastq.gz" "ERR031026_2.fastq.gz")

# Function to check if an element is in an array
containsElement () {
  local element match="$1"
  shift
  for element; do [[ "$element" == "$match" ]] && return 0; done
  return 1
}

# Loop through each FASTQ file in the directory
for FASTQ_FILE in "${FASTQ_DIR}"/*_1.fastq.gz; do

    # Extract the base name of the FASTQ file without the _pass1.fastq.gz part
    BASENAME=$(basename "${FASTQ_FILE}" "_1.fastq.gz")
   
    # Define paired file names
    PASS1_FILE="${FASTQ_DIR}/${BASENAME}_1.fastq.gz"
    PASS2_FILE="${FASTQ_DIR}/${BASENAME}_2.fastq.gz"

    # Check if either file is in the exclusion list
    if containsElement "${PASS1_FILE}" "${EXCLUDE_FILES[@]}" || containsElement "${PASS2_FILE}" "${EXCLUDE_FILES[@]}"; then
      echo "Skipping ${BASENAME} pair"
      continue
    fi
   
    # Define output file names
    OUTPUT_PASS1="${OUTPUT_DIR}/${BASENAME}_cleaned1.fastq.gz"
    OUTPUT_PASS2="${OUTPUT_DIR}/${BASENAME}_cleaned2.fastq.gz"
    UNPAIRED1="${OUTPUT_DIR}/${BASENAME}_1.unpaired.fastq.gz"
    UNPAIRED2="${OUTPUT_DIR}/${BASENAME}_2.unpaired.fastq.gz"
    REPORT_JSON="${OUTPUT_DIR}/${BASENAME}_report.json"
    HTML_REPORT="${OUTPUT_DIR}/${BASENAME}_report.html"
   
    # Run fastp with specified parameters
    fastp --in1 "${PASS1_FILE}" \
          --in2 "${PASS2_FILE}" \
          --out1 "${OUTPUT_PASS1}" \
          --out2 "${OUTPUT_PASS2}" \
          --unpaired1 "${UNPAIRED1}" \
          --unpaired2 "${UNPAIRED2}" \
          --average_qual 28 \
          --trim_front1 10 \
          --trim_tail1 10 \
          --json "${REPORT_JSON}" \
          --html "${HTML_REPORT}"
   
    echo "Processed ${BASENAME} pair -> ${OUTPUT_PASS1}, ${OUTPUT_PASS2}"
done
```

In this code we trimmed 10 base pairs from the head and the tail because in the multiqc we saw a lower quality in these areas. In class, we learned that in Illumina sequencing the quality of the first base pairs is lower, as well as the quality is getting lower at the end of the sequence. Furthermore, it is common to maintain a quality score of 30 according to fastqc calculation, but in order to preserve as much data as we can without comprising the quality we used a quality score of 28 as seen in the multiqc as the threshold value. # Alignment

In the same manner, we performed an alignment to the human genome with a bash code that uses bwa-mem command (from bwa tool), together with flagstat from samtools to see how the alignment worked, on the processed data as described below:   

```{r, engine='bash', Performing bwa mem on the processed data using a the following bash code}
#!/bin/bash

# Set the directory containing the fastq files
READS_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/processed_fastq"

# Output directory for the alignment files
OUTPUT_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/bam_files"
mkdir -p $OUTPUT_DIR

# List of sample IDs
SAMPLE_IDS=("ERR031027" "ERR031028" "ERR031029" "ERR031030" "ERR031031" "ERR031032" "ERR031033" "ERR299297" "ERR299298" "ERR299299" "ERR031035" "ERR031038" "ERR031039" "ERR031040" "ERR031041" "ERR031042" "ERR031043" "ERR031044" "ERR031017" "ERR031018" "ERR031019" "ERR299295" "ERR299296" "ERR031022" "ERR031023" "ERR031024")  

# Loop through each sample ID
for SAMPLE_ID in "${SAMPLE_IDS[@]}"; do
    # Define the paths for R1 and R2 files based on the sample ID
    R1="${READS_DIR}/${SAMPLE_ID}_pass_1.fastq"
    R2="${READS_DIR}/${SAMPLE_ID}_pass_2.fastq"
   
    # Output SAM file path
    OUTPUT_BAM="${OUTPUT_DIR}/${SAMPLE_ID}_aligned.bam"
   
    # Run bwa mem
    bwa mem "/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/hg38.fa.bwt" $R1 $R2 | samtools view -Sb -> $OUTPUT_BAM

    # Sort the BAM file
    samtools sort $OUTPUT_DIR/${SAMPLE_ID}_aligned.bam -o $OUTPUT_DIR/${SAMPLE_ID}_aligned_sorted.bam

    # Index the sorted BAM file
    samtools index $OUTPUT_DIR/${SAMPLE_ID}_aligned_sorted.bam
    
    # Do flagstat to file
    samtools flagstat $OUTPUT_DIR/${SAMPLE_ID}_aligned_sorted.bam
done
```

After a successful alignment, we want to identify genetic variations and how they might effect the manifestation of the disease. Hence, we used bcftools for variant calling with the following code:

```{r, engine='bash', Variant calling bash code}
#!/bin/bash

# Define the input and output directories and the reference genome
REFERENCE="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/hg38.fa"
INPUT_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/bam_files"
OUTPUT_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/bcf_files"

# Create the output directory if it doesn't exist
mkdir -p $OUTPUT_DIR

# Loop through all BAM files in the input directory
for BAM_FILE in $INPUT_DIR/*.bam; do
 # Extract the base name of the BAM file (without directory and extension)
 BASE_NAME=$(basename $BAM_FILE .bam)

 # Define the output BCF file path
 BCF_FILE="${OUTPUT_DIR}/${BASE_NAME}.bcf"

 # Perform variant calling
 bcftools mpileup -Ou -f $REFERENCE $BAM_FILE | bcftools call -mv -Ob -o $BCF_FILE

 # Index the BCF file
 bcftools index $BCF_FILE

 echo "Variant calling completed for $BAM_FILE. Results are in $BCF_FILE"
done

echo "All variant calling processes are completed."
```

Out of the variants found, we need only those with a quality score above 30 and those with a depth of coverage greater than 10. This threshold enables the balance between ensuring high confidence in the variant calls while retaining a reasonable number of variants for analysis, as well as threshold of 10 ensures that the variant is supported by a sufficient number of reads, reducing the likelihood of calling a variant based on sequencing errors. 

```{r, engine='bash', Filtering in order to have high quality variants bash code}
#!/bin/bash

# Directory containing your BCF files
INPUT_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/bcf_files"
OUTPUT_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/filtered_bcf_files"

# Create output directory if it doesn't exist
mkdir -p "$OUTPUT_DIR"

# Loop over each BCF file in the input directory
for bcf_file in "$INPUT_DIR"/*.bcf; do
   # Extract the base name of the file (without directory and extension)
   base_name=$(basename "$bcf_file" .bcf)

   # Define the output file name
   output_file="$OUTPUT_DIR/${base_name}.filtered.bcf"

   # Apply the filter: QUAL > 30 and DP > 10
   bcftools filter -i 'QUAL>30 && DP>10' -Oz -o "$output_file" "$bcf_file"

   # Index the filtered BCF file
   bcftools index "$output_file"

   echo "Processed and indexed: $bcf_file -> $output_file"
done

echo "All files processed."
```

As requested in the assignment, we merged the healthy samples as well as the sick in two separate files (and added the group name to each file accordingly) using bcftools merge function in a bash code for all samples: 

```{r, engine='bash', Merge the healthy and sick samples}
#!/bin/bash

# Directories and file paths
BCF_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/filtered_bcf_files"
HEALTHY_SUFFIX="_healthy"
SICK_SUFFIX="_sick"
MERGED_HEALTHY="merged_healthy.bcf"
MERGED_SICK="merged_sick.bcf"

# List of healthy sample identifiers (without file extensions)
healthy_ids=("ERR031027" "ERR031029" "ERR031031" "ERR031033" "ERR031035" "ERR299299" "ERR031039" "ERR031041" "ERR031043" "ERR031017" "ERR031019" "ERR299296" "ERR031023" "ERR031025")

# Function to check if an element is in an array
contains() {
  local e
  for e in "${@:2}"; do [[ "$e" == "$1" ]] && return 0; done
  return 1
}

# Create arrays to hold the filenames for merging
healthy_files=()
sick_files=()

# Rename files and categorize them
for file in "$BCF_DIR"/*.bcf; do
  filename=$(basename "$file")
  base="${filename%.*}"
  identifier="${base%%_*}"
 
  if contains "$identifier" "${healthy_ids[@]}"; then
    new_name="${base}${HEALTHY_SUFFIX}.bcf"
    mv "$file" "$BCF_DIR/$new_name"
    bcftools index "$BCF_DIR/$new_name"
    healthy_files+=("$BCF_DIR/$new_name")
  else
    new_name="${base}${SICK_SUFFIX}.bcf"
    mv "$file" "$BCF_DIR/$new_name"
    bcftools index "$BCF_DIR/$new_name"
    sick_files+=("$BCF_DIR/$new_name")
  fi
done

# Merge healthy samples
if [ ${#healthy_files[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
  bcftools merge -O b -o "$BCF_DIR/$MERGED_HEALTHY" "${healthy_files[@]}"
  bcftools index "$BCF_DIR/$MERGED_HEALTHY"
fi

# Merge sick samples
if [ ${#sick_files[@]} -gt 0 ]; then
  bcftools merge -O b -o "$BCF_DIR/$MERGED_SICK" "${sick_files[@]}"
  bcftools index "$BCF_DIR/$MERGED_SICK"
fi

echo "Merging complete."
```

Now, we'll use bcftools view to filter and edit variant calling format (VCF) with the flags: -v snps in order that the file will only include SNPs (Single Nucleotide Polymorphisms); -O b to have the output format as binary BCF; and -o that defines the output file where the filtered SNPs will be saved. Then, we created an index for the BCF or VCF file using bcftools index to make querying and accessing data faster.

```{r, engine='bash', Filter only SNP's}
bcftools view -v snps /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/filtered_bcf_files/merged_healthy.bcf -O b -o healthy_snps.bcf 
bcftools view -v snps /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/filtered_bcf_files/merged_sick.bcf -O b -o  sick_snps.bcf
bcftools index /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/healthy_snps.bcf
bcftools index /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/sick_snps.bcf 
```

Our next step was to compare the two BCF files and find unique variants present in one file but not the other using bcftools isec with the flags -C that selects variants that are unique to the sick sample but not in the healthy one, and -p to specify the output directory where the result of the intersection will be stored. 

```{r, engine='bash', Intersecting SNP's between the healthy and sick samples}
bcftools isec -C /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/sick_snps.bcf /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/healthy_snps.bcf -p /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/intsichea
```

This results in a complied VCF file of the results that now we'll intersect with known clinical variants using bedtools intersect to find overlaps. We used the -v flag in order the the output file will include only the lines from 0000.vcf that didn't overlap with any features in SNPs.ClinVar.JAN24.bed, resulting in the exclution of common variants; the -a and -b flags to indicate which file to include the results of the intersection process; and the -header flag that ensures the VCF header is preserved in the output.

```{r, engine='bash', Finding novel somatic variants}
gunzip -c /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/SNPs.ClinVar.JAN24.bed.gz > SNPs.ClinVar.JAN24.bed
bedtools intersect -v -a /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/intsichea/0000.vcf -b SNPs.ClinVar.JAN24.bed -header > somatic_novel_newnew.vcf
```

We used the result of the previous command and used bedtools intersect to find novel somatic variants overlaps with flags that we previously explained.

Now, we'll Use Salmon to quantify per-sample expression levels. Hence, we first downloaded the reference fasta and indexed it. 

```{r, engine='bash', Salmon script}
#!/usr/bin/env bash

# Directory containing your FASTQ files
FASTQ_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/after_fastp"

# Output directory for processed FASTQ files
OUTPUT_DIR="/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/salmon"

# Create output directory if it doesn't exist
mkdir -p "${OUTPUT_DIR}"

# Samples
accessions=("ERR031027" "ERR031028" "ERR031029" "ERR031030" "ERR031031" "ERR031032" "ERR031033" "ERR299297" "ERR299298" "ERR299299" "ERR031035" "ERR031038" "ERR031039" "ERR031040" "ERR031041" "ERR031042" "ERR031043" "ERR031044" "ERR031017" "ERR031018" "ERR031019" "ERR299295" "ERR299296" "ERR031022" "ERR031023" "ERR031024")

for acc in "${accessions[@]}"; do
  echo salmon quant -i /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hg38_refGene_index -l A -1 "${FASTQ_DIR}/${acc}_cleaned1.fastq.gz" -2 "${FASTQ_DIR}/${acc}_cleaned2.fastq.gz" -p 8 --validateMappings -o "${OUTPUT_DIR}/${acc}"
  salmon quant -i /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hg38_refGene_index -l A -1 "${FASTQ_DIR}/${acc}_cleaned1.fastq.gz" -2 "${FASTQ_DIR}/${acc}_cleaned2.fastq.gz" -p 8 --validateMappings -o "${OUTPUT_DIR}/${acc}"
done
```

Then, we executed salmon quantify on all of our accessions to quantify transcript abundances from RNA-seq data, adding the -i flag to specify the directory containing the pre-built Salmon index; the -l flag to select library type A- automatic one, allowing Salmon to infer the library type from the data; flags -1 and -2 specifies the first and second the paired-end reads sets (forward and reverse reads, accordingly) in FASTQ format; -p flag to select 8 threads to use in mapping; and --validateMappings flag in order that Salmon will validate read mappings to the reference, and by that improve the accuracy by correcting potential mismatches between reads and the reference transcriptome.

```{r, engine='bash', Merge Salmon's result to one file}
python /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/transcript_to_gene.py /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/TranscriptToGene.hg38.tsv /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/salmon /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/out_file_merged.tsv 
```

The salmon quantify gives an output of a directory of files each of one belonging to one sample. In order to perform a broader scale analysis, we'll use the script
transcript_to_gene.py to obtain one file containing the per-sample per-gene reads
counts and TPM levels.

```{r, engine='bash', PyDESeq2 differential expression analysis}
from pathlib import Path
import os
import pickle as pkl

from pydeseq2.dds import DeseqDataSet
from pydeseq2.default_inference import DefaultInference
from pydeseq2.ds import DeseqStats
from pydeseq2.utils import load_example_data
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import dash_bio
import plotly.express as px

out_dir = Path("/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/salmon")
out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)  # Create path if it doesn't exist

# Data loading
# Update this path to the appropriate location on your system
counts_file = Path("/Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/out_file_merged.tsv")

counts_df = (
    pd.read_table(counts_file)
    .pivot(
        columns="Gene",
        index="Sample",
        values="NumReads"
    )
    .sort_index()
    .astype(int)
)

metadata = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "Sample": [
            "Normal", "Tumor", "Normal", "Tumor", "Normal", "Tumor",
            "Normal", "Tumor", "Normal", "Tumor", "Normal", "Tumor",
            "Normal", "Tumor", "Normal", "Tumor", "Normal", "Tumor",
            "Normal", "Tumor", "Normal", "Tumor", "Normal", "Tumor",
            "Normal", "Tumor"
        ]
    },
    index=[
        "ERR031027", "ERR031028", "ERR031029", "ERR031030", "ERR031031", "ERR031032",
        "ERR031033", "ERR299297", "ERR031035", "ERR299298", "ERR299299", "ERR031038",
        "ERR031039", "ERR031040", "ERR031041", "ERR031042", "ERR031043", "ERR031044",
        "ERR031017", "ERR031018", "ERR031019", "ERR299295", "ERR299296", "ERR031022",
        "ERR031023", "ERR031024"
    ]
)

# Preprocessing
samples_to_keep = ~metadata["Sample"].isna()
counts_df = counts_df.loc[samples_to_keep]
metadata = metadata.loc[samples_to_keep]

genes_to_keep = counts_df.columns[counts_df.sum(axis=0) >= 10]
counts_df = counts_df[genes_to_keep]

# Ensure indices are sorted and aligned
counts_df = counts_df.sort_index()
metadata = metadata.sort_index()

print("Counts DataFrame indices:")
print(counts_df.index)

print("Metadata indices:")
print(metadata.index)

# DeseqDataSet Initialization
inference = DefaultInference(n_cpus=8)
dds = DeseqDataSet(
    counts=counts_df,
    metadata=metadata,
    design_factors="Sample",
    refit_cooks=True,
    inference=inference,
)

# Running DESeq2
dds.deseq2()
print(dds)

# Statistical Analysis
stat_res = DeseqStats(dds, inference=inference)
stat_res.summary()

dds.varm["LFC"]

stat_res_df = stat_res.results_df.reset_index()
stat_res_df["-log10(padj)"] = -np.log10(stat_res_df["padj"])

# Significant Genes
significantly_changed_genes = stat_res_df.loc[
  (stat_res_df["log2FoldChange"].abs() >= 2) &
    (stat_res_df["-log10(padj)"] >= -np.log10(0.00005)),
  ["Gene"]
]
print(significantly_changed_genes['Gene'])
significantly_changed_genes.to_csv("significantly_changed_genes.csv", index=False)
positively_significantly_changed_genes = stat_res_df.loc[
  (stat_res_df["log2FoldChange"] >= 2) &
    (stat_res_df["-log10(padj)"] >= -np.log10(0.00005)),
  ["Gene"]
]
print(positively_significantly_changed_genes['Gene'])
positively_significantly_changed_genes.to_csv("positively_significantly_changed_genes.csv", index=False)
# Define the cutoffs
log2fc_cutoff = 2
padj_cutoff = -np.log10(0.00005)

# Create a new column 'regulation' to categorize the genes
stat_res_df["regulation"] = "Not Significant"
stat_res_df.loc[
    (stat_res_df["log2FoldChange"] >= log2fc_cutoff) & 
    (stat_res_df["-log10(padj)"] >= padj_cutoff), 
    "regulation"
] = "Upregulated"
stat_res_df.loc[
    (stat_res_df["log2FoldChange"] <= -log2fc_cutoff) & 
    (stat_res_df["-log10(padj)"] >= padj_cutoff), 
    "regulation"
] = "Downregulated"

# Volcano Plot
fig = px.scatter(
    stat_res_df,
    x="log2FoldChange",
    y="-log10(padj)",
    color="regulation",  # Color by the regulation column
    title="A volcano plot demonstrating the significance of change in<br>expression due to cancer",
    hover_data=["Gene"],
    color_discrete_map={
        "Upregulated": "blue", 
        "Downregulated": "red", 
        "Not Significant": "gray"
    }  # Define the colors for each category
)

# Add lines for cutoffs
fig.add_shape(
    type="line",
    x0=-log2fc_cutoff, x1=-log2fc_cutoff,
    y0=0, y1=stat_res_df["-log10(padj)"].max(),
    line=dict(color="red", width=2, dash="dash"),
)
fig.add_shape(
    type="line",
    x0=log2fc_cutoff, x1=log2fc_cutoff,
    y0=0, y1=stat_res_df["-log10(padj)"].max(),
    line=dict(color="red", width=2, dash="dash"),
)
fig.add_shape(
    type="line",
    x0=stat_res_df["log2FoldChange"].min(), x1=stat_res_df["log2FoldChange"].max(),
    y0=padj_cutoff, y1=padj_cutoff,
    line=dict(color="black", width=2, dash="dash"),
)

# Update layout and save
fig.update_layout(template="plotly_white", width=600, height=400)
fig.write_image(Path(out_dir, "VolcanoPlot.png"), width=600, height=400)
fig.show()
```

In order to use PyDESeq2 for differential expression analysis, we used a code previously used in the class exercise ??? with minor modifications. To conclude the project, we want to combine our insights from novel somatic variants and differentially expressed genes in prostate cancer. We took only positively significantly changed genes (from step 7), and counted the number of novel somatic variants (from step 5) per each such gene. To link the gene symbols of the positively significantly changed genes to their gene ID equivalents (file 4) and use that to link these genes to their coordinates in the genes bed file (file 2), we used the awk command to reformat the GeneIDGeneSymbol.txt file to a refined workable version. Meaning, we used a comma (,) as the field separator (-F","), with the condition of NR > 1 to ensure that the operation is performed only on lines after the header row,as well as the gsub function to remove all double-quote characters (") from the first and second fields ($1 and $2, accordingly). Then, we used grep to search for lines in cleaned_gene_symbl.txt that match any Gene Symbol or ID listed in positively_significantly_changed_genes.txt, and write the matching lines to gene_id_gene_symbl.txt using the -F option to interpret the fixed strings, and the -f option to specify a file containing the needed patterns. This was followed by an additional awk command to match the gene symbols between two files to output their corresponding Gene IDs along with genomic coordinates. It reads the first file (gene_id_gene_symbl.txt) to map Gene Symbols to Gene IDs. Then, for each Gene Symbol in the second file (Genes.RefSeq.JAN24.bed), it checks for a match in the first file and prints the chromosome, start, and end positions from the second file, along with the Gene ID, into a new file (genesCoordinates1.bed). The command ensures tab-separated formatting and adds placeholders for the score (.) and strand (+) fields. With the new bed file formed, we used bedtools sort to rearrange the coordinated before the bedtools merge. Despite the assignment's requirement to use bedtools merge -i <path_to_file> -s -c 4,5,6 -o distinct, sum,distinct, we received time and again the following error: Unrecognized parameter: sum,distinct. Hence, we used the bedtools merge -i genesCoordinates_sorted1.bed -c 4,6 -o distinct,distinct -delim ";" -s command to intersect the merged gene coordinates with the novel somatic variants from VCF file and count the number of SNPs per interval. Meaning, the bedtools merge command merges overlapping or adjacent genomic intervals from the input file genesCoordinates_sorted1.bed, using the -s flag to ensure that only intervals on the same strand are merged, the -c 4,6 flag to specify that columns 4 (Gene IDs) and column 6 (strand) should be retained from the merged intervals, the -o distinct,distinct flag that only unique values are kept for these columns and the -delim ";" flag to set the semicolon as the separator between multiple distinct values in the output file. To find overlapping regions between the two files: the gene intervals in genesCoordinates_sortmX.bed and the somatic variants in somatic_novel_newnew.vcf, we used the bedtools intersect command as previously explained. We want to count the number of unique Gene IDs from the file containing overlapping gene intervals and somatic variants, thus, we used the awk command. We printed the fourth column ($4) that corresponds to the Gene IDs, sorted them alphabetically,and with uniq -c counted the occurrences of each unique Gene ID, outputting the count alongside each ID, sorting them in descending order. 

```{r, engine='bash', Count SNP's per gene}
awk -F"," 'NR > 1 { gsub(/"/, "", $1); gsub(/"/, "", $2); print $2 "\t" $1}' /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/GeneIDGeneSymbol.txt > cleaned_gene_symbl.txt
awk -F"," 'NR > 1 {gsub(/"/, "", $1); print $1}' positively_significantly_changed_genes.csv > positively_significantly_changed_genes.txt
grep -Ff positively_significantly_changed_genes.txt cleaned_gene_symbl.txt > gene_id_gene_symbl.txt
awk 'BEGIN {FS=OFS="\t"} NR==FNR {a[$2]=$1; next} $4 in a {print $1, $2, $3, a[$4], ".", "+"}' gene_id_gene_symbl.txt /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/hw5/Genes.RefSeq.JAN24.bed > genesCoordinates1.bed
bedtools sort -i genesCoordinates1.bed > genesCoordinates_sorted1.bed
bedtools merge -i genesCoordinates_sorted1.bed -c 4,6 -o distinct,distinct -delim ";" -s > genesCoordinates_sortmX.bed
bedtools intersect -a genesCoordinates_sortmX.bed -b /Users/dr.juliamonte-cristo/somatic_novel_newnew.vcf -wa -wb > genesCoordinates_sortmX_snps.bed
awk '{print $4}' genesCoordinates_sortmX_snps.bed | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr > genesCoordinates_sortmX_snps.txt
```

Using the awk command, we identified duplicate Gene IDs from the file genesCoordinates_sortmX_snps.txt, sorted alphabetically and filtered with uniq -d those that appear more than once in the input file as follows: 

```{r, engine='bash', Gene Coordinates}
awk '{print $2}' genesCoordinates_sortmX_snps.txt | sort | uniq -d
```

This process didn't yield results, meaning the SNP's count show unique genetic regions. 
The gene that showed the largest number of SNP's somatic mutations was the PCA3 gene, also known as Prostate cancer antigen 3 (PCA3). This gene is a prostate cancer-specific long noncoding RNA (lncRNA) that is known to play a role in prostate cancer progression that is mediated by nucleoplasmic lamins. Furthermore, PCA3 is also known to be involved in the control of prostate cancer cell survival and modulates cancer-related genes. Experiments also showed that PCA3 was involved in the control of chromatin organization in several genomic regions as well as that its expression levels can be an effective predictor of malignant prostate cancer (1). Hence, increased expression levels of PCA3 may indicate on extensive modulation of cancer-related genes, that prompts the prostate cancer's progression.

```{r, echo=FALSE, fig.cap="Fig. 5b,c from ref. 1-high expression of PCA3", out.width = '100%'}

```

We couldn't find enough research paper explaining the connection between the high expression levels of PCA3 the creation of somatic mutations in that gene. However, we did find research papers showing the connection between lncRNA and somatic mutations in different types of cancer. One of them (2) showed that somatic mutations can act through lncRNAs to enhance pathological cancer cell fitness. This may explain the high expression levels of PCA3 together with the novel somatic SNP's mutations found.
